subject: Business
source: Gap-fill against Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Business 4BS1 specification

lessons.title: Why motivation matters to a business
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a business gain when its workers want to do a good job?
objectives: Define motivation and explain how it helps a business attract and retain employees
Explain how motivation improves productivity
Calculate labour turnover and productivity to judge the effect of motivation
successCriteria: All: define motivation and state two benefits to a business
Most: calculate productivity and labour turnover
Some: evaluate whether a motivation scheme is worth its cost
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages and ratios; PSHE: wellbeing at work
lessons.smsc: Social and moral: sincerity of intention (ikhlas) and fair, respectful treatment of staff

keywords.def: the desire or willingness of employees to work hard and do a good job
output per worker in a given time
keeping employees so that they stay with the business
the percentage of employees who leave in a year
employees missing work without good reason

starter: Name two types of employment.
State one reason for equal opportunities law.
What is the difference between recruitment and selection?

teach.heading: What is motivation?
bullets: The reason an employee chooses to work hard
Motivated staff care about quality and customers
Low motivation means mistakes, lateness and absence
Motivation comes from pay and from how people are treated
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Noor Printing, twelve staff who print and deliver orders. Ask: when did you last work hard on something? What made you want to? Elicit pay, recognition, interest, being trusted, being treated fairly. Link to intentions: the same work done with sincerity and care tends to be better work. The theories of Herzberg, Maslow and Taylor and the pay and non-pay methods come in another lesson; today is about why it matters.

teach.heading: Benefits to the business
teach.note: Use the cycle. Walk round it: motivated staff stay longer, so the business spends less on recruiting and training; experienced staff produce more and better work; better quality pleases customers; more sales support pay and a good workplace. Attract: a business with a good reputation as an employer receives more and better applicants. Retain: fewer leavers.
cycle: They work harder and stay longer
Customers are happier and sales grow
The business can afford better rewards

teach.heading: Worked example: measuring the effect
teach.note: Model both formulas. Productivity = output / number of employees. Labour turnover (%) = leavers in the year / average number of employees x 100 (a common formula, not listed in the spec: say so, and use as extension). Discuss what 15 per cent means: about one in seven leave each year. Then discuss cost: each leaver costs advertising, interview time and training. Do not quote real averages.

model.problem: Noor Printing has 40 employees on average. Six leave this year. Before a new reward scheme, 12 printers produce 3,000 orders a month. After, the same 12 produce 3,300. Calculate labour turnover, and productivity before and after.
model.answer: Labour turnover is 15 per cent; productivity rose from 250 to 275 orders per printer, a 10 per cent increase.

teach.heading: Check: attract and retain
teach.note: Answer B. Retaining means keeping employees. A is about recruiting new staff; C is a cost saving that has nothing to do with staying; D is about productivity not retention. Ask pupils to reword the true statement in their own words.

check.q: Which situation best shows motivation helping a business RETAIN employees?
options: More people apply for a job after an advert
Fewer experienced workers resign this year than last year
The business moves to a cheaper building
A worker completes more orders in an hour
check.why: Retaining means keeping workers, shown by fewer resignations. More applicants is attraction and more orders per hour is productivity.

teach.heading: Is it always worth it?
bullets: Rewards cost money, time and effort
A scheme must raise output or cut leavers to pay off
Not everyone is motivated by the same things
Fair treatment costs little but matters a lot
teach.note: Evaluation slide. Calculate for the class: if a scheme costs 6,000 pounds a year and replacing one leaver costs about 2,500 pounds (invented figure), the scheme pays for itself if it prevents three leavers. Ask: what else would you want to know? (Whether the leavers left for pay or for other reasons, how productivity changes.) Remind them that motivation also needs trust and respect, not just money.

practice: Calculate productivity: 4,500 meals made by 15 chefs in a week.
A cafe has 25 staff on average and 5 leave in a year. Calculate labour turnover.
Explain one reason a motivated workforce might lower costs for a business.
independent: Core: Copy and complete the cycle for a halal restaurant: show how motivated staff can lead to higher profit.
Extend: Explain two ways motivation helps a business attract and retain employees (4 marks).

Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): a bakery spends 8,000 pounds a year on bonuses and free meals. Productivity rises 6 per cent and two fewer staff leave. Is the spending justified? State what else you need to know.
exit: Define motivation.
Write the productivity formula.
Big question: one reason a business gains from motivated workers.
lessons.homework: Interview a family member about a job they enjoyed. Write what motivated them and how it affected their work.
lessons.send: SEND: give the formulae on cards and a step-by-step calculation frame. EAL: use pictures for retain, attract. Stretch: explore why money alone may not retain staff.

lessons.title: Human resources: planning, training, safety and industrial relations
lessons.bigQuestion: What does a business need to do to look after the people who make it work?
objectives: Describe the main tasks of the human resources department
Explain workforce planning, training, health and safety, welfare, employment issues and industrial relations
Calculate staffing needs for workforce planning
successCriteria: All: list six HR tasks
Most: explain two HR tasks using an example
Some: calculate staffing needs and judge the effect of poor industrial relations
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: calculating staff numbers; PSHE: safety and wellbeing
lessons.smsc: Moral: duty of care and fair dealing towards employees

keywords.def: working out how many staff, with which skills, the business needs
protecting people from injury and illness at work
looking after employees' wellbeing
the relationship between employers and employees or their representatives
an organisation that represents workers and negotiates with employers
matters such as contracts, pay, hours and working conditions

starter: What is productivity and how is it calculated?
Give two ways a business can motivate staff.
State one benefit of using part-time staff.

teach.heading: The HR department
teach.note: Bismillah. In a small business the owner does these jobs; in larger businesses there is a human resources (HR) department, one of the main functional areas. Context: fictional Safa Logistics, a delivery firm with 60 staff. Ask pupils to guess what HR does, then reveal the table. Recruitment and selection and training are covered in other lessons, so today link, not repeat.

head: HR task
What it involves
Example at Safa Logistics
rows: Decide how many staff and which skills are needed
Plan extra drivers before a busy period
Rest breaks, quiet room, counselling support
Meet the union about new shift times

teach.heading: Worked example: workforce planning
teach.note: Model the calculation: required hours divided by hours per worker. Then ask: what if two staff are off sick or a seasonal peak? Workforce planning is not just a number: it covers skills too (do they have licences to drive? first aid?). Discuss the cost of hiring too few (late deliveries, stressed staff) and too many (wasted wages).

model.problem: Safa Logistics expects 780 hours of delivery work a week in the busy period. Each full-time driver works 30 hours a week on the road. It has 22 drivers. How many more drivers does it need?
steps: Drivers needed = total hours / hours per driver
model.answer: Safa Logistics needs 4 more drivers (for example seasonal or temporary staff).

teach.heading: Health, safety and welfare
bullets: Employers have a legal duty to protect workers
Risk checks, safety training and protective equipment
Welfare goes beyond safety: breaks, support, facilities
Safe, cared-for staff work better and leave less often
teach.note: Do not quote specific legislation unless you can verify it; in the UK the main law is the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 (verify). The idea to teach: employers must provide a safe workplace. Welfare examples: rest areas, drinking water, flexibility for prayer times where practical, counselling help lines, sick pay. Link to the Islamic ethic of caring for those in your charge, as a value, not a ruling.

teach.heading: Industrial relations and employment issues
bullets: Good relations mean talking and listening to staff
Trade unions negotiate pay and conditions for members
Poor relations can lead to strikes and lost output
Contracts and fair conditions prevent disputes
teach.note: Define a trade union and collective bargaining (a union negotiates with the employer for a group of workers). Use the two outcomes: good industrial relations (regular meetings, listening, fair pay deals) versus poor (rumours, working to rule, strike). Discuss costs of a strike: lost production, late deliveries, damaged reputation, lost wages. Employment issues: written contract, hours, holidays, overtime, pay, promotion routes.

teach.heading: Check: which HR task?
teach.note: Answer C. Meeting union representatives to discuss shift patterns is industrial relations. A is health and safety, B is workforce planning, D is training. Ask pupils which keyword in the stem gave it away.

check.q: Safa Logistics' managers meet union representatives to agree new shift times. Which HR task is this?
check.why: Discussions with workers' representatives about conditions are industrial relations. The others deal with safety, numbers of staff or skills.

teach.heading: Linking HR to the rest of the business
teach.note: Use this as the plenary slide to link to other departments: finance (wages and budgets), marketing (staff who deal with customers need training), production (safe machines and skilled workers). Ask how a decision by HR to cut training could affect production and finance later. Revisit the big question and list the tasks pupils think matter most.
bullets: HR works with every other department
Training affects quality and safety
Workforce plans affect the wage budget
Poor welfare affects productivity and turnover

practice: List four tasks of the HR department.
Calculate: 450 hours of work needed; each worker gives 25 hours. Workers needed?
Explain one way good industrial relations help a business.
independent: Core: Match seven HR tasks to seven scenarios for a halal restaurant.
Extend: Explain two ways a business could improve staff welfare and one benefit of each (6 marks).
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): a factory has poor industrial relations and a rising number of accidents. Which HR task should the owner tackle first? Justify your choice.
exit: Name three HR tasks.
Define industrial relations.
Big question: one way a business looks after its people.
lessons.homework: Choose a business you know. Write one example for each of five HR tasks that the business must carry out.
lessons.send: SEND: card-sort for HR tasks with pictures. EAL: pre-teach welfare, relations, planning. Stretch: weigh the cost of safety measures against the cost of an accident.

lessons.title: Human resources: discipline, grievance, dismissal and redundancy
lessons.bigQuestion: How can an employer deal fairly with problems at work, even when someone must leave?
objectives: Distinguish disciplinary action, grievance, dismissal, unfair dismissal and redundancy
Explain why a fair procedure matters
Calculate the cost and saving of making staff redundant
successCriteria: All: define the five terms
Most: decide whether a scenario is fair dismissal, unfair dismissal or redundancy
Some: evaluate the effects of redundancy on a business
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: employment rights; Maths: cost and payback calculations
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice ('adl), honouring agreements and treating people with dignity

keywords.def: steps an employer takes when an employee breaks the rules
a formal complaint by an employee about their treatment at work
the employer ends an employee's contract for a valid reason
dismissal without a valid reason or without a fair procedure
a job is no longer needed, so the employee is let go through no fault of their own
breaking workplace rules

starter: Define industrial relations.
Name three HR tasks.
What is the aim of health and safety law?

teach.heading: Discipline and grievance
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Amanah Care Home, 35 staff. Two directions: discipline is employer to employee (breaking rules); grievance is employee to employer (complaining). Typical disciplinary steps: informal talk, verbal warning, written warning, final warning, dismissal. A fair process includes telling the employee the problem, hearing their side, allowing a companion and an appeal. Exact legal procedures differ by country; in the UK there is an ACAS code of practice (verify before quoting details).

right.title: Grievance
points: Examples: bullying, unsafe conditions, unfair treatment

teach.heading: Dismissal, unfair dismissal, redundancy
teach.note: Distinguish carefully; this is where pupils lose marks. Dismissal can be fair: for example serious misconduct, repeated lateness after warnings, or persistent poor performance after support. Unfair dismissal: no valid reason, no proper procedure, or a reason such as discrimination or joining a union. Redundancy: the JOB disappears, perhaps because demand fell or a machine replaced it. It is not about the person, so the employee is usually entitled to redundancy pay (in the UK this depends on age and length of service; verify the formula before using it).

head: Term
Reason
Fair?
Example
rows: Fair if valid reason and procedure
Stealing from the till after proper investigation
No valid reason or unfair procedure
Sacked without warning for raising a safety complaint
Fair if genuine and handled properly

teach.heading: Check: which term?
teach.note: Answer D. The role disappears for business reasons: redundancy. A needs conduct; B would be unfair; C is a grievance. Make sure pupils say 'the job, not the person'.

check.q: A care home closes a wing and no longer needs six night-shift posts. Which term describes the staff losing their jobs?
check.why: The jobs are no longer needed, so it is redundancy. Disciplinary and unfair dismissal concern the employee's conduct or an unfair reason, and a grievance is a complaint by the employee.

teach.heading: Worked example: the cost of redundancy
teach.note: Model the calculation. It is invented data to show the payback idea. Emphasise the hidden costs not in the calculation: loss of skills and experience, lower morale among remaining staff, reputation, and possible difficulty recruiting again if demand returns. Link to the exam: 'evaluate' needs both sides.

model.problem: A care home plans to make 5 staff redundant. Redundancy pay is 1,500 pounds each. Each employee costs 1,800 pounds a month in wages. How long before the saving covers the redundancy cost?
model.answer: One-off cost 7,500 pounds; monthly saving 9,000 pounds; payback in under one month. But morale, skills and service quality also matter.

teach.heading: Why fair procedures matter
bullets: Fair treatment keeps morale and trust high
Unfair dismissal can lead to a tribunal and compensation
Clear records protect both sides
Honouring agreements and being just is an ethical duty
teach.note: Discuss the cost of getting it wrong: legal costs, compensation, a poor reputation, other staff worried. Islamic ethos: justice and keeping promises and contracts are central values in Islamic ethics; use as a principle without citing specific texts unless verified. Practise a short discussion: should a manager dismiss a long-serving employee for one late arrival without any warning?

practice: Define grievance and give one example.
State the difference between dismissal and redundancy.
Calculate: 3 redundancies at 2,000 pounds each; each wage is 2,200 pounds a month. Payback time?
independent: Core: Sort eight short scenarios into disciplinary, grievance, fair dismissal, unfair dismissal and redundancy.
Extend: Explain two effects on the remaining staff when a business makes people redundant (4 marks).
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): a restaurant with falling sales can make four waiters redundant or cut everyone's hours. Which is better for the business? Justify.
exit: Define redundancy.
Why is unfair dismissal costly to a business?
Big question: one way to handle a workplace problem fairly.
lessons.homework: Write a one-paragraph reply from a manager to an employee who has raised a grievance about a long shift rota, using a fair approach.
lessons.send: SEND: scenario cards with colour-coded categories. EAL: pre-teach dismissal, redundancy, grievance. Stretch: compare UK legal protections with those in another country using verified sources.

lessons.title: The finance department: wages, budgets, cash flow and accounts
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a business keep control of its money from day to day?
objectives: Describe the main tasks of the finance department
Calculate wages, a monthly salary, a closing cash balance and a budget variance
Explain how finance interacts with other departments
successCriteria: All: list four finance tasks
Most: calculate wages and a cash-flow closing balance
Some: explain how a budget helps control costs and evaluate its limits
lessons.smsc: Moral: trustworthiness (amanah) in handling money and keeping honest records

keywords.def: pay usually based on hours worked, often paid weekly
a fixed yearly amount, usually paid monthly
a prediction of money coming in and going out each month
a financial plan for future income and spending
the difference between budgeted and actual figures
recording and reporting a business's financial transactions

starter: Define labour turnover.
Name two HR tasks.
What is the difference between profit and cash?

teach.heading: What does finance do?
bullets: Pays wages and salaries on time and correctly
Forecasts cash flow to avoid shortages
Sets budgets and compares them with actual results
Keeps accounts and reports to owners and the tax authority
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Bilal's Print and Copy, with 8 staff. Finance is one of the four main functional areas. In a small firm the owner or an accountant carries these tasks. Link to trustworthiness: money entrusted to a business must be recorded honestly. Ask which tasks help the owner to decide and which tasks are about legal duty (accounts, tax).

teach.heading: Worked example: wages and salary
teach.note: Model gross wage = hours x rate, then monthly salary = annual salary / 12. Overtime: say 'paid at time and a half' as an invented rate. Do not state legal overtime rules. Discuss why a wage suits shift work and a salary suits a manager whose hours vary, and who is more costly to the business in a busy period.

model.problem: A print operator works 35 hours at 12 pounds an hour plus 6 overtime hours at time and a half. A manager earns 30,000 pounds a year, paid monthly. Find the operator's weekly pay and the manager's monthly pay.
steps: Overtime rate = 12 x 1.5 = 18 pounds an hour
model.answer: Operator 528 pounds a week; manager 2,500 pounds a month (before tax).

teach.heading: Cash-flow forecasts and budgets
teach.note: Show the table, which is a one-month forecast. Closing balance = opening balance + receipts - payments. The closing balance of one month becomes the opening of the next. A budget is the plan: 'we expect to spend 6,000 on materials'. Variance = actual - budget; spending above budget means costs are higher than planned. Ask pupils to explain why a business can be profitable and still run out of cash (customers pay late; large payments due). Link to the cash flow lesson.

teach.heading: Check: budget variance
teach.note: Answer A. 6,800 - 6,000 = 800 above budget, so costs are higher than planned. B reverses it, C is the budget, D is the actual figure. Pupils should say 'actual minus budget' and state whether it is above or below.

check.q: Bilal budgeted 6,000 pounds for paper in March. He actually spent 6,800 pounds. What is the variance?
check.why: Actual minus budget = 6,800 - 6,000 = 800, so spending is 800 pounds higher than planned. 800 below would need actual to be 5,200.

teach.heading: Accounting and working with other departments
bullets: Accounts record sales, costs and assets
Used for tax, loans and decisions by owners
Marketing, HR and production all depend on finance budgets
Honest records protect trust with banks and customers
teach.note: Accounting means recording transactions and preparing financial statements (covered in the financial documents unit). Link: marketing bids for an advertising budget; production asks for money to replace a machine; HR asks for training funds. Finance decides within what the business can afford. Evaluation prompt: what are the dangers of setting a budget too tight? (Staff cannot do their jobs.) Too loose? (Waste.) Honest records matter: a business should not hide figures from the tax authority or investors.

practice: Calculate weekly wage: 40 hours at 9.50 pounds an hour.
Calculate monthly salary for 27,600 pounds a year.
Opening balance 1,500, receipts 6,000, payments 5,200. Closing balance?
independent: Core: Complete a three-month cash-flow table for a halal market stall using given receipts and payments.
Extend: Explain two ways a budget helps a business control costs (4 marks).
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): a small firm's forecast shows a negative closing balance in March. Recommend two actions and judge which is better.
exit: List three tasks of the finance department.
Write the closing balance formula.
Big question: one way a business controls its money.
lessons.homework: Write a one-week personal budget with income and spending, then calculate the variance if spending was higher than planned.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-printed forecast tables with the formula on a card. EAL: pre-teach receipts, payments, variance. Stretch: calculate variance as a percentage of budget.

lessons.title: Marketing and production departments: what they do and how they connect
lessons.bigQuestion: How do the marketing and production departments work together to deliver what customers want?
objectives: Describe the roles of the marketing department
Describe the roles of the production department
Calculate a reorder level and explain how departments depend on each other
successCriteria: All: list tasks of marketing and of production
Most: explain how quality control and stock control help the business
Some: evaluate what happens when marketing and production do not communicate
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: calculations with stock levels; D&T: design and quality
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty in advertising and care for quality in what we sell

keywords.def: deciding which products to make and how to improve them
short-term offers to boost sales
helping customers before and after they buy
managing the business's image with the public and media
checking that products meet the standard
managing inventory so there is enough without waste
the stock level at which new supplies are ordered

starter: Name two tasks of the finance department.
Define variance.
State one reason a business uses market research.

teach.heading: What marketing does
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Yasmin's Granola, a halal-certified cereal maker, selling to supermarkets and online. Marketing ties together much of what pupils learned in unit 4: research, product, price, promotion, place, packaging. Ask pupils to give one real example for each task from Yasmin's. Customer service includes answering queries and handling complaints; public relations is managing how people view the business, for example a story in the local paper.

head: Marketing task
What it involves
Example at Yasmin's Granola
rows: Set prices to suit customers and costs
Introductory price for a new flavour
Donate boxes to a local food bank and tell the local press
Recyclable box; supply to shops and online

teach.heading: What production does
bullets: Manufacturing: making the product efficiently
Designing new products with marketing and finance
Quality control: checking standards before products leave
Stock control: enough materials, no waste
teach.note: Production is the department that makes the goods (or provides the service). Designing new products relies on market research from marketing and on cost limits from finance. Quality control means inspecting samples or finished products and acting on faults: a faulty batch reaching customers damages reputation. Stock control means keeping enough raw materials and finished stock to meet orders without storing too much, which ties up cash and may spoil (an issue for food).

teach.heading: Worked example: reorder level
teach.note: Model the simple formula reorder level = (daily usage x lead time) + buffer stock. Lead time is the time between ordering and delivery. The buffer stock is a safety margin. Check pupils understand that ordering at the reorder level means stock lasts until delivery, with the buffer unused unless something goes wrong. Link to cash: too much stock ties up money, and spoilt food is wasted, which is also an ethical concern.

model.problem: Yasmin's uses 40 kg of oats a day. Oats take 3 days to be delivered. She keeps a buffer stock of 60 kg. At what stock level should she reorder?
model.answer: Reorder when oat stock falls to 180 kg.

teach.heading: Check: which department?
teach.note: Answer B. Working out a safe level of oats and when to reorder is stock control, a production task. A is marketing research, C is finance, D is HR. Ask pupils to give the signal word 'reorder'.

check.q: Which department task is working out when to reorder oats so the factory never runs out?
check.why: Managing stock levels and ordering is stock control, which belongs to production. The other options are different department tasks.

teach.heading: Departments must communicate
teach.note: Case: marketing runs a big promotion, but production is not told. Orders double and the factory cannot keep up, causing late deliveries and angry customers. Reverse case: production makes a lot of an unpopular flavour because it has not seen marketing research. Discuss what would help: regular meetings, shared forecasts, clear information. Honesty point: marketing should not promise what production cannot deliver, and advertising claims must be true.
bullets: Marketing forecasts demand, production plans output
Finance sets the budget for both
Quality problems hurt marketing and customer service
Poor communication wastes money and loses customers

practice: List four tasks of the marketing department.
Reorder level: usage 25 kg a day, lead time 4 days, buffer 30 kg.
Explain one problem if production does not know about a planned promotion.
independent: Core: Sort fourteen tasks into marketing, production, finance and HR for a halal food factory.
Extend: Explain two ways quality control protects a food business's reputation (4 marks).
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): to cut costs, production reduces quality checks. Is this a good decision? Consider customers, costs and reputation.
exit: Name three marketing tasks and three production tasks.
Define stock control.
Big question: one way marketing and production help each other.
lessons.homework: Choose a food brand. Describe one thing its marketing department and one thing its production department must do for the brand to succeed.
lessons.send: SEND: department task cards with icons. EAL: pre-teach lead time, buffer, quality control. Stretch: calculate the cost of too much stock using a storage cost per kg.

lessons.title: Using the income statement: decisions and the importance of profit
lessons.bigQuestion: If sales go up, why might profit go down?
objectives: Use the statement of comprehensive income (income statement) to make decisions
Calculate gross profit and operating profit
Explain the nature and importance of profit
successCriteria: All: state the formulae for gross and operating profit
Most: compare two years and identify why profit changed
Some: evaluate decisions a business could take using the figures
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentage change; Economics: profit and incentives
lessons.smsc: Moral: lawful (halal) earnings, honest accounts and the fair treatment of customers and staff

keywords.def: a financial statement showing revenue, costs and profit over a period
money earned from selling goods or services
the direct costs of the goods sold
sales revenue minus cost of sales
running costs not included in cost of sales, such as rent and wages
gross profit minus expenses

starter: Define revenue.
Name one fixed cost and one variable cost.
Give the formula for profit.

teach.heading: Reading the income statement
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Rayyan's Halal Butchers. Construction of the statement is not required in the exam, but pupils must read and use it. Walk down the table: sales revenue, less cost of sales equals gross profit, less expenses equals operating profit. Note that the specification calls it the statement of comprehensive income; many businesses say income statement or profit and loss account. Pupils need the two profit lines.

teach.heading: Worked example: why profit fell
teach.note: Model the calculations in order. Percentage change = change / original x 100. Sales up 20 per cent but cost of sales up 30 per cent: the cost of meat and supplies grew faster than sales. Gross profit grew only 5 per cent. Expenses grew 12.5 per cent. Operating profit fell 10 per cent. Discuss decisions: negotiate with suppliers, adjust prices, reduce waste, control expenses. Emphasise using numbers in an answer.

model.problem: Using the table, find the percentage change in sales and in operating profit between Year 1 and Year 2, and say what it shows.
steps: Sales change = (180,000 - 150,000) / 150,000 x 100 = 20 per cent increase
Operating profit change = (18,000 - 20,000) / 20,000 x 100 = -10 per cent
Cost of sales rose 30 per cent (27,000 / 90,000), faster than sales
model.answer: Sales rose 20 per cent but operating profit fell 10 per cent because costs rose faster than revenue.

teach.heading: Using it to decide
bullets: Compare with earlier years to spot trends
Compare gross and operating profit to find where costs rise
Set prices and cost-saving targets
Support a bank loan or investor request
teach.note: Decision-making: a business uses the statement to see where problems are. If gross profit is weak, look at supplier prices, prices charged and waste. If gross profit is fine but operating profit is weak, expenses are the problem. A bank will look at profit to judge whether a loan can be repaid. Ask pupils what Rayyan should look into first and why. Remind them that one year's figures need to be compared with other years or other businesses.

teach.heading: Check: profit calculation
teach.note: Answer C. Gross profit = 80,000 - 50,000 = 30,000; operating profit = 30,000 - 22,000 = 8,000. A is gross profit; B subtracts expenses from revenue skipping cost of sales wrongly; D adds. Show on the board.

check.q: Revenue is 80,000 pounds, cost of sales 50,000 pounds and expenses 22,000 pounds. What is operating profit?
check.why: Gross profit is 80,000 - 50,000 = 30,000. Operating profit = 30,000 - 22,000 = 8,000. 30,000 is only the gross profit.

teach.heading: The nature and importance of profit
bullets: Profit is what is left after costs are paid
It rewards the owners for risk and effort
It can be reinvested to grow the business
It attracts investors and helps secure loans
teach.note: Define profit as revenue minus total costs. Importance: survival (continual losses cannot be sustained), reward for owners, retained profit for growth, confidence for lenders and investors, and funds for pay and community activity. Profit is not the only aim: some businesses are social enterprises. Islamic ethos: trade and earning a fair profit are permitted and praised as ethical enterprise when done honestly; profit must come from lawful, fair dealing, with honest weights and descriptions. Present as general principle only and avoid detailed rulings or quotations unless verified by a scholar.

teach.heading: Misconception: profit is not cash
teach.note: Reinforce the difference. Profit comes from the income statement; cash is the money actually in the bank. Revenue can be recorded when a sale is made but cash may arrive later. A profitable business can still run out of cash if customers pay late or large payments fall due. Link to the cash flow lesson and the liquidity lesson next.

misconception.wrong: If the income statement shows a profit, the business must have plenty of cash.
misconception.right: Profit and cash are different. A business can be profitable but short of cash if customers pay late or it has bought a lot of stock.

practice: Calculate gross profit: revenue 45,000, cost of sales 28,000.
Calculate operating profit if expenses are 9,000.
Give two reasons why profit is important to a business.
independent: Core: Use a given two-year income statement for a halal cafe to calculate gross and operating profit for both years.
Extend: Explain how a business could use its income statement to decide whether to raise prices (4 marks).
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): sales rose 12 per cent but operating profit fell. The owner proposes cutting staff. What else should be investigated first? Reach a judgement.
exit: Write the formulae for gross profit and operating profit.
Give one reason profit is important.
Big question: one reason profit can fall when sales rise.
lessons.homework: Using a business of your choice, invent a simple income statement for two years and write three sentences comparing them.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn statement with colour-coded lines and formula cards. EAL: pre-teach revenue, expenses, profit. Stretch: calculate profit margins and compare.

lessons.title: Liquidity: why a business needs to pay its bills on time
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can a profitable business still collapse?
objectives: Explain the concept of liquidity
Calculate the current ratio and acid test ratio
Explain why liquidity matters and how a business can improve it
successCriteria: All: define liquidity and say why it matters
Most: calculate the current ratio and acid test ratio
Some: evaluate how a business could improve its liquidity position
lessons.smsc: Moral: fulfilling obligations and paying debts on time, a widely valued principle in Islamic ethics

keywords.def: a business's ability to pay its short-term debts
assets likely to be turned into cash within a year, such as inventory, receivables and cash
debts due within a year, such as payables and overdrafts
current assets divided by current liabilities
current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities
stock of goods and materials held

starter: Define operating profit.
Write the formula for gross profit.
Why can profit differ from cash?

teach.heading: What is liquidity?
bullets: Can the business pay what it owes soon?
Cash is the most liquid asset
Inventory takes time to sell, so it is less liquid
Profit does not guarantee liquidity
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Madinah Mini Market. Ask: if a supplier asks to be paid tomorrow and the business has stock but little cash, what can it do? Liquidity is about the short term: can it pay wages, suppliers and bills as they fall due? Link to the unit on cash flow. A business can be profitable but illiquid. Islamic ethos: paying what you owe on time is a widely held ethical value; present as a principle.

teach.heading: Two liquidity ratios
teach.note: In the exam the formulae are supplied, but pupils must use them correctly, so practise. Current assets: inventory, receivables (customers who owe money) and cash. Current liabilities: payables (money owed to suppliers), overdraft and other debts due within a year. The acid test removes inventory because it is the slowest to turn into cash. Typical guidance: a current ratio around 1.5 to 2 is often seen as comfortable and an acid test of about 1 or above is safer, but these depend on the type of business, so avoid presenting them as laws.

head: Ratio
Formula
What it tells us
rows: Can short-term debts be covered by short-term assets?
Can debts be paid without selling stock?

teach.heading: Worked example: calculating both ratios
teach.note: Model carefully. Show the steps and the interpretation: 2.0 looks healthy but the acid test shows only 0.71, so without selling stock Madinah would struggle to pay all current debts at once. Ask pupils to say it in a sentence. For a supermarket-style business, stock turns quickly so a low acid test may be less worrying; this is a good evaluation point.

model.problem: Madinah Mini Market has inventory 18,000, receivables 6,000 and cash 4,000 (pounds). Its payables are 10,000 and overdraft 4,000. Calculate the current ratio and acid test ratio.
model.answer: Current ratio 2.0; acid test ratio 0.71: it relies on selling stock to pay all its debts.

teach.heading: Check: acid test
teach.note: Answer A. (50,000 - 20,000) / 15,000 = 2.0. B forgets to subtract inventory (that is the current ratio 3.33). C divides the wrong way round. D subtracts liabilities. Insist on writing the formula first.

check.q: A shop has current assets of 50,000 pounds including inventory of 20,000 pounds, and current liabilities of 15,000 pounds. What is the acid test ratio?
check.why: Acid test = (50,000 - 20,000) / 15,000 = 2.0. 3.3 is the current ratio because inventory has not been removed.

teach.heading: Why liquidity matters, and improving it
bullets: Poor liquidity can mean unpaid wages and suppliers
Suppliers may stop supplying; the business may fail
Too much liquidity means idle cash that could be used
Improve: chase receivables, cut stock, negotiate longer credit, arrange an overdraft
teach.note: Discuss both extremes. Too low: risk of insolvency, even when profitable. Too high: cash or stock sitting unused could be reinvested. Ways to improve: speed up payment by customers, reduce excess inventory, negotiate longer payment terms with suppliers (watch the relationship), arrange a short-term loan or overdraft (has a cost), sell an unused asset. Ask which is best for the mini market and why. Comparing liquidity with earlier years and other businesses is covered in the accounts-analysis lesson.

practice: Calculate the current ratio: current assets 36,000, current liabilities 24,000.
Calculate the acid test ratio if inventory is 12,000 in the same business.
Explain one reason why inventory is excluded in the acid test ratio.
independent: Core: Given a short list of balance sheet items for a halal bakery, identify current assets and liabilities and calculate both ratios.
Extend: Explain two ways a business could improve its liquidity and one drawback of each (6 marks).
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): a firm has a current ratio of 3.5 and an acid test of 0.6. Is its liquidity good? What further information would you want?
exit: Define liquidity.
Write the acid test formula.
Big question: why can a profitable business still collapse?
lessons.homework: Write a short note explaining to a shop owner, in plain English, the difference between profit and liquidity, using one numerical example.
lessons.send: SEND: formula cards and a colour-coded balance sheet list. EAL: pre-teach liquid, debt, payable, receivable. Stretch: discuss why supermarkets can run with low liquidity ratios, with justification.
